# Peter Lynch: One Up On Wall Street

Source: [One-Up-on-Wall-Street-By-Peter-Lynch.md](../../../../../One-Up-on-Wall-Street-By-Peter-Lynch.md)

## 1. Core Philosophy

- **Amateur advantage:** individuals can find tenbaggers (10×) before Wall Street by watching their job, industry, and shopping habits. Professionals are slowed by bureaucracy, rules against small or unknown companies, and fear of looking wrong.
- **Invest in what you know, then do the homework.** A product you like is only a lead; the stock is a buy only after checking the numbers.
- **Long-term, earnings drive price.** The stock price line eventually follows the earnings line. Short-term moves are noise.
- **Don't time the market or forecast the economy.** Predicting the market over one or two years is impossible; stay invested and keep picking good companies. Market declines are buying opportunities.
- Millennium intro: corrections (≥10%) come every couple of years, bear markets (≥20%) about every six. Don't hold stocks with money needed in the next 12 months.
- Stocks have beaten bonds and T-bills by wide margins over long periods, despite crashes.
- You don't need to be right most of the time: being right **6 times out of 10** gives an excellent record, because winners can rise 10× while losers lose at most 100%.
- Magellan (1977–90): ~29%/yr.

## 2. Readiness: Before Buying Stocks (Ch. 3–5)

1. **Own a house first** (if you intend to); it's a good leveraged investment that most people do well in.
2. **Only invest money you won't need** for years; you shouldn't be forced to sell at a bad time.
3. **Personal qualities:** patience, self-reliance, common sense, tolerance for pain, open-mindedness, detachment, persistence, humility, flexibility, willingness to do independent research, willingness to admit mistakes, ability to ignore general panic.
- Don't ask "Is the market going up?" Ask "Is this company a good investment at this price?"

## 3. The Six Categories (Ch. 7)

Classify every stock. Category determines expectations, what to check, and when to sell. Companies move between categories over time.

| Category | Growth | What to expect | How to play | Key checks |
|----------|--------|----------------|-------------|------------|
| **Slow grower** | ~2–4%/yr (≈ GNP) | Dividend, little upside | Buy for dividend; sell after 30–50% gain or fundamentals worsen | Dividend paid consistently and raised; payout ratio; ability to pay in recessions |
| **Stalwart** | ~10–12%/yr | 30–50% gains over 1–2 yrs; good recession protection | Buy at reasonable P/E, sell after 30–50%, rotate into another undervalued stalwart | P/E vs historical range; diworseification; long-term growth rate; how it did in past recessions |
| **Fast grower** | 20–25%+/yr | Tenbaggers possible (10–40×+) | Hold while growth and expansion continue | Main product a big % of sales; success duplicated in new markets; room to grow; P/E near growth rate; expansion speeding up or slowing; few institutions own it |
| **Cyclical** | Rises/falls with economy (autos, airlines, steel, chemicals) | Big gains if bought near bottom, 50%+ losses if bought at top | Timing is everything; buy when business is terrible and improving; know the industry | Inventories, supply/demand, new entrants, P/E (low P/E at peak earnings is a trap) |
| **Turnaround** | Battered, near-bankrupt | Fast large recovery if it survives; little tied to market | Buy when survival is likely and the fix is identifiable | Cash vs debt, debt structure; how it's turning around (dumping losers, cutting costs, new products); is business coming back |
| **Asset play** | Any | Hidden value the market overlooks | Buy below asset value; wait for value to be recognized (often via a raider/sale) | What assets are worth; hidden assets; debt reducing them; new share issuance; raider interest |

- Examples: slow growers = utilities; stalwarts = Coca-Cola, P&G, Bristol-Myers; fast growers = Taco Bell, Walmart, The Limited, La Quinta; cyclicals = Ford, Chrysler (later); turnarounds = Chrysler, Lockheed, Penn Central, GPU; asset plays = Pebble Beach, Alico, railroads with land, cable/TV/cellular franchises, tax-loss carryforwards.
- Fast growers eventually become stalwarts or slow growers; turnarounds become cyclicals or stalwarts once fixed.
- Fast growers' risk: overexpansion, poor financing, and the P/E collapse when growth slows (Sensormatic $42 → $5.6).
- Kinds of turnaround: bail-out-or-bust (Chrysler), the unexpected (Con Ed), perceived troubles that aren't real (Three Mile Island's GPU), restructuring to maximize shareholder value.
- Hidden assets: land at old book values, natural resources, brand/franchises, cash, tax-loss carryforwards, valuable subsidiaries, cable/cellular/TV licenses, pension overfunding.

## 4. The Perfect Stock: 13 Traits (Ch. 8)

1. Sounds dull, or even ridiculous (Pep Boys, Bob Evans Farms).
2. Does something dull (Crown Cork & Seal, ADP).
3. Does something disagreeable (Safety-Kleen, Envirodyne).
4. It's a spinoff (Toys "R" Us; Baby Bells).
5. Institutions don't own it and analysts don't follow it.
6. Rumors abound: toxic waste and/or the Mafia (Waste Management).
7. There's something depressing about it (Service Corporation International, funerals).
8. It's a no-growth industry (no competition flood).
9. It's got a niche (gravel pits, drug patents, dominant local newspapers/TV, brands).
10. People have to keep buying it (drugs, soft drinks, razor blades, cigarettes).
11. It's a user of technology, not a maker (supermarket using scanners; ADP).
12. Insiders are buyers (especially middle managers buying with their own money).
13. The company is buying back shares.

## 5. Stocks to Avoid (Ch. 9)

- **Hottest stock in the hottest industry:** attracts competitors; profits vanish.
- **The "next" something** (the next IBM, the next McDonald's): the copy rarely works.
- **Diworseification:** profitable companies blowing cash on overpriced, unrelated acquisitions. Prefer buybacks or higher dividends.
- **Whisper stocks:** long-shot stories with no earnings ("it's a sure thing").
- **The middleman:** supplier selling 25–50% of output to one customer; that customer has huge leverage.
- **Exciting name** on a mediocre company: attracts buyers but gives false comfort.

## 6. Earnings & P/E (Ch. 10)

- Stock prices follow earnings over time. Find earnings and price lines; when price is far above the earnings line, be careful; far below, investigate.
- P/E = years to earn back the price at constant earnings. It's a quick gauge of overpricing.
- Average P/E varies by category: slow growers low, stalwarts higher, fast growers highest. Compare P/E with the company's own history and industry.
- Extreme P/Es punish even good companies: McDonald's at 50× in 1972 went sideways for years; Polaroid, Avon at 50–64× fell 80%+.
- Market P/E context: when the general market P/E is very high (e.g., 1987), be more selective.
- Earnings future depends on five ways a company grows: reduce costs, raise prices, expand into new markets, sell more in old markets, revitalize/close/sell a losing operation.

## 7. Two-Minute Drill & Getting the Facts (Ch. 11–12)

- Before buying, be able to give a **two-minute monologue**: why you're interested, what has to happen for success, and the pitfalls. Different for each category, e.g.:
  - Slow grower: dividends paid for X years, raised regularly, payout manageable.
  - Stalwart: P/E near low end of range, new products or growth drivers, no major problems.
  - Cyclical: industry conditions improving; inventories, capacity, pricing trends.
  - Fast grower: where growth comes from, how far expansion can go.
  - Turnaround: how it's getting better (cost cuts, asset sales, new products), and survival.
  - Asset play: what the assets are worth, how much the stock reflects them, any raiders.
- Sources: broker/analyst reports, Value Line, S&P sheets, the company's investor relations (call with specific questions), visiting stores/HQ, annual reports (focus on balance sheet and numbers, not the glossy pages), 10-K, 10-Q.
- Lavish headquarters are a bad sign; frugal ones good (Crown Cork & Seal vs Uniroyal; Taco Bell behind a bowling alley).
- Ask management about specifics: inventories, new store results, capacity, margins, buybacks. Expect a surprise in maybe 1 call in 10; that's where the edge is.

## 8. Famous Numbers (Ch. 13)

| Number | Rule / insight |
|--------|----------------|
| **% of sales** | A hot product matters only if it's a big share of sales or profits (L'eggs for Hanes yes; a single drug for a giant, often no). |
| **P/E vs growth** [verified] | P/E ≈ growth rate is fair. P/E ½ of growth = very positive; 2× growth = very negative. 12% grower at P/E 6 attractive; 6% grower at P/E 12 unattractive. |
| **Dividend-adjusted ratio** [verified] | (Long-term growth % + dividend yield %) ÷ P/E. <1 poor, 1.5 okay, ≥2 what you want. 15% + 3% ÷ 6 = 3 (fabulous). |
| **Cash position** | Net cash (cash + securities − long-term debt) per share lowers the real price. Ford 1987: $16.30 net cash/share on a $38 stock, plus finance units ≈ $16.60, so the auto business cost ~$5.10 for ~$7 of EPS. |
| **Debt factor** [verified] | Normal balance sheet ≈ 75% equity / 25% debt. Ford: ~91% equity. Weak: 80% debt / 20% equity. Debt decides who survives a crisis. |
| **Bank vs funded debt** | Bank debt is due on demand, so it's dangerous. Funded debt (long-term bonds, can't be called) gives time to recover. GCA (bank debt, little cash) failed; Applied Materials (cash > debt) recovered. |
| **Dividends** | Companies that pay dividends tend to be less prone to frivolous acquisitions. Look for 20–30-yr records of uninterrupted, rising dividends. Payout ratio shows cushion; heavy debt + small companies risk dividend cuts. |
| **Book value** | Often overstated (inventories and specialized plant worth far less in a sale) or understated (land, brands, licenses at old cost). Inspect what's behind it. |
| **Hidden assets** | Land, natural resources, brands, subsidiaries, tax-loss carryforwards, licenses, overfunded pensions. |
| **Cash flow** | Check if earnings are backed by cash. Cash flow 10:1 (price ÷ cash flow per share) is standard; a 20% cash return is terrific. Use **free cash flow** (cash flow after capex). Coastal: $7/share FCF on a $20 stock. |
| **Inventories** | Inventories growing faster than sales = red flag (products not selling). In depressed companies, inventories starting to drop = first sign of turnaround. Watch LIFO vs FIFO. |
| **Pension plans** | Check that pension assets exceed vested benefits; underfunding is a hidden liability (Bethlehem Steel). |
| **Growth rate** | Earnings growth (ideally from raising prices without losing customers) is what matters. A 20% grower at 20× P/E beats a 10% grower at 10×: $1 EPS becomes $6.19 vs $2.59 in 10 years. Growth > 25–30% rarely lasts. |
| **Pretax profit margin** | Avg corporate ~5% (examples: Ford 10.3%, Albertson's 3.6%, Merck 25%). For long-term holds, want high-margin companies (survive price cuts); for turnarounds/recoveries, low-margin companies gain most when business improves. |

## 9. Rechecking the Story (Ch. 14)

- Recheck every few months: earnings, P/E vs growth, and whether the story is still true.
- Fast-grower life phases: **start-up** (riskiest), **rapid expansion** (safest, where most money is made), **maturity/saturation** (growth slowing, stock re-rates down).
- Key question for a retailer/restaurant: how much room left to expand (e.g., The Limited in X of Y malls)?

## 10. Final Checklist by Category (Ch. 15)

**All stocks:** P/E (high or low vs history and industry); % institutional ownership (lower better); insiders buying; company buying back shares; record of earnings growth and whether sporadic or consistent; strong balance sheet (debt/equity, financial strength rating); cash position (net cash per share is a floor).

- **Slow growers:** steady dividends, regularly raised; payout ratio low enough to withstand bad times.
- **Stalwarts:** P/E vs normal range; possible diworseifications reducing future earnings; long-term growth rate maintained; how it fared in past recessions/market drops.
- **Cyclicals:** watch inventories and supply/demand; new entrants (bad); P/E shrinking as recovery matures and earnings peak; know the cycle; upturn easier to spot than downturn.
- **Fast growers:** product is a big part of business; growth rate in past years (20–25% is ideal, be wary >25%); success duplicated in another city/town; room to grow; P/E at or near growth rate; expansion speeding up (or at least not slowing); few institutions own it, few analysts.
- **Turnarounds:** can it survive a creditor raid? Cash vs debt; debt structure; if bankrupt, what's left for shareholders; how it's turning around (eliminating unprofitable divisions, cutting costs); is business coming back.
- **Asset plays:** asset value; hidden assets; debt that offsets assets; new debt or share issuance diluting assets; raider interest.

## 11. Portfolio Design (Ch. 16)

- Realistic expectation: market ~9–10%/yr long-term; a good stock picker aims for 12–15% after costs. Expecting 30% leads to reckless bets.
- Small investor: **3–10 stocks** you understand well; own as many as you have true edge and research for.
- Mix by category to balance risk: Lynch's Magellan ≈ 30–40% fast growers, 10–20% stalwarts, 10–20% cyclicals, rest special situations/turnarounds/asset plays.
- Rotate within categories: sell stalwarts after 30–50% gains, buy cheaper ones; several 30% moves compound like a big winner.
- **Don't pull the flowers and water the weeds:** don't sell winners early and hang onto losers. Add to winners whose story is improving.
- Don't use stop-loss orders (e.g., 10%); they lock in losses on good companies at the worst time.
- Never go fully to cash because of market fears.

## 12. When to Buy & Sell (Ch. 17)

**Good buying times:** year-end tax-loss selling (Oct–Dec); market collapses, corrections, crashes (Oct 1987), when good companies get dumped with the bad.

**Sell signals by category:**
- *Slow grower:* gained 30–50% or fundamentals worsen; lost market share for two years; no new products, less R&D; diworseifying acquisitions; heavy debt; dividend no longer covered.
- *Stalwart:* P/E well above normal range (e.g., 15 when peers are 11–12); no insider buying for a year; new products disappointing or a major division (≈25% of earnings) vulnerable; growth slowing while costs already cut.
- *Cyclical:* near end of cycle; costs rising; plants running at full capacity and company spending to add more; inventories building, can't get rid of them; commodity prices falling; futures below spot; new competitors; union contracts expiring with demands; demand slowing; capex doubled for a fancy new plant; can't compete with foreign producers.
- *Fast grower:* end of rapid-expansion phase; same-store sales declining; new stores disappointing; top executives leaving; stock P/E far above realistic growth (e.g., 30× vs 15–20% growth); heavy institutional ownership and analyst coverage (e.g., 40 analysts, 60% institutional); management on a road show to many cities; magazine covers praising the CEO.
- *Turnaround:* after it has turned around and everyone knows it (Chrysler at $48); debt rising after shrinking for several quarters; inventories rising twice as fast as sales; P/E inflated vs earnings prospects; strongest division sells to one big customer.
- *Asset play:* wait for a raider or value realization. Warnings: management issues 10% more shares to diversify; a division sold for far less than expected; a tax cut reducing the value of loss carryforwards; institutional ownership rising sharply (from ~25% to 60%), meaning the "secret" is out.

Beware fake sell signals: "extended" chart talk, takeover rumors, the drumbeat of macro worries.

## 13. The Twelve Silliest (and Most Dangerous) Things People Say (Ch. 18)

1. "If it's gone down this much already, how much lower can it go?" (Polaroid, Kaiser)
2. "You can always tell when a stock's hit bottom." (falling knife)
3. "If it's gone this high already, how can it possibly go higher?" (Philip Morris kept rising)
4. "It's only $3 a share: what can I lose?" (100%, same as any stock)
5. "Eventually they always come back." (RCA, Johns-Manville didn't)
6. "It's always darkest before the dawn." (oil rigs, freight cars kept falling)
7. "When it rebounds to $10, I'll sell."
8. "What, me worry? Conservative stocks don't fluctuate much." (utilities crashed)
9. "It's taking too long for anything to happen." (Merck flat for years, then soared; big gains often come in years 3–4)
10. "Look at all the money I've lost: I didn't buy it!" (unrealized "losses" on stocks you didn't own aren't losses)
11. "I missed that one, I'll catch the next one." (the copycat usually disappoints)
12. "The stock's gone up, so I must be right," or "...gone down, so I must be wrong." (price moves don't validate a thesis)

## 14. Options, Futures, Shorting, News (Ch. 19–20)

- Lynch never bought futures or options; most amateurs (80–95% by his estimate) lose on them. Options expire, and the fee/time decay works against you; futures are zero-sum.
- Portfolio insurance amplified the 1987 crash.
- Shorting: unlimited loss potential, dividends owed, margin calls; even if right eventually, a short squeeze can ruin you (Resorts International).
- Big news and macro events often matter less to stocks than expected, and vice versa. Don't trade on headlines.
- Institutional herding: when everyone owns and praises a stock, most of the move is over.

## 15. Consolidated Numeric Rules

| Rule | Threshold | Ch. |
|------|-----------|-----|
| Slow grower growth | ~2–4% | 7 |
| Stalwart growth / target gain | ~10–12% / 30–50% then rotate | 7, 16 |
| Fast grower growth | 20–25% ideal; wary > 25% | 7, 15 |
| P/E vs growth | ½ = very good; 1× = fair; 2× = very bad | 13 |
| (g + yield) / P/E | < 1 poor; 1.5 okay; ≥ 2 good; 3 fabulous | 13 |
| Normal debt structure | ~25% debt / 75% equity | 13 |
| Price/cash flow | ~10:1 standard | 13 |
| Pretax margin | avg corporate ~5% | 13 |
| Middleman risk | 25–50% of sales to one customer | 9 |
| Success rate needed | ~6 of 10 picks | intro |
| Realistic return target | 12–15%/yr | 16 |
| Small portfolio size | 3–10 stocks | 16 |
| Stop-loss | Don't use | 16 |

## 16. Key Takeaways (closing summary, verbatim bullets)

- "Market declines are great opportunities to buy stocks in companies you like."
- "To come out ahead you don't have to be right all the time, or even a majority of the time."
- "You can make serious money by compounding a series of 20–30 percent gains in stalwarts."
- "Just because a company is doing poorly doesn't mean it can't do worse."
- "Buying a company with mediocre prospects just because the stock is cheap is a losing technique."
- "Selling an outstanding fast grower because its stock seems slightly overpriced is a losing technique."
- "A stock does not know that you own it."
- "You won't improve results by pulling out the flowers and watering the weeds."
- "If you don't think you can beat the market, then buy a mutual fund and save yourself a lot of extra work and money."
- "Any idiot can run this business" is one characteristic of the perfect company.
